brand.title: ESourceAIG (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — ESource WhiteLabel Sales Course

questions.question: What are the three main reasons that firms buy the ESource white-label bookkeeping tool?
choices: Bank feeds, payroll integration, and mobile app access
Their brand, data stays home, and lower cost per client
Client login portal, unlimited staff seats, and AI suggestions
QuickBooks integration, Xero compatibility, and Wave support
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—brand, data privacy, and cost savings are the core value propositions that win deals.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While some of those features exist, they're not the three main reasons firms buy. The course emphasizes brand visibility, data privacy (statements staying on the firm's computers), and per-client pricing advantages over competitors.

questions.question: What is the ideal firm size and type for the ESource white-label tool?
choices: Large CPA firms with over 200 monthly clients
Solo bookkeepers with fewer than 5 clients
Bookkeeping and small CPA firms with roughly 5 to 100 monthly clients
Firms that specialize in payroll and tax services only
questions.feedback_correct: You've identified the exact fit: bookkeeping and small CPA firms in the 5–100 client range who value their own brand and client privacy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course is clear that the sweet spot is firms with about 5 to 100 monthly clients. Firms smaller than 5 or much larger than 100, or those with different priorities, may not be the best fit.

questions.question: During the discovery phase, which four topics should you ask the prospect about?
choices: Their budget, their office location, their staff count, and their IT vendor
Today's tools, cost, brand, and time spent chasing clients
Their competitors, their growth plans, their accounting methods, and their software licenses
Their client retention rate, their pricing model, their geographic region, and their industry focus
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—these four discovery questions uncover the pain points that your demo and close will later address.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course outlines a specific discovery framework: ask about the software clients use, how price increases have affected them, whose name appears on reports, and how many hours go to chasing transactions. These reveal real pain.

questions.question: How long should the product demo last, and what is the first thing you show?
choices: 30 minutes, starting with the pricing calculator
10 minutes, starting with the bank feeds integration
15 minutes, starting with the firm-branded screen
20 minutes, starting with the Ask Client tab
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—keep it tight at 15 minutes and lead with their brand on screen; that's the moment that sells.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes a 15-minute demo that opens with the firm-branded screen (ideally with their logo already added). This visual brand moment is what captures attention first.

questions.question: What happens when a bookkeeper clicks 'Text client' in the Status tab for a missing statement?
choices: The system sends an automated text immediately to the client
A message opens ready to send from the bookkeeper's own phone, with the missing statement already listed
The system generates a formal email on behalf of the firm
The client receives a calendar reminder on their phone automatically
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the message is pre-populated and ready to send from the bookkeeper's personal number, which resonates because it solves a real monthly pain point.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course shows that 'Text client' opens a pre-filled message ready to send from the bookkeeper's own phone. The system doesn't send automatically; the bookkeeper controls the send, which gives the firm confidence.

questions.question: When pricing the tool for a firm with 38 active client books, how are the rates applied?
choices: All 38 books are charged at the average rate of $15 per book
All 38 books are charged at $20 each
Each rate applies only to the books in its band: $20 for the first, $17 for clients 2–10, $15 for 11–30, and $14 for 31–38
The firm pays a flat monthly fee regardless of client count
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—pricing is tiered like tax brackets, so each band's rate applies only to the books in that band, which keeps larger firms' costs lower per book.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The pricing structure is graduated, not flat or averaged. For 38 books, you'd calculate: 1×$20 + 9×$17 + 20×$15 + 8×$14. Always use the pricing calculator to avoid math errors.

questions.question: How should you handle the objection 'Our clients already know QuickBooks'?
choices: Explain that your tool is easier to learn than QuickBooks
Agree and switch the conversation to a different topic
Point out that clients get Excel reports with the firm's name and don't need to learn any software
Offer free training for all the firm's clients
questions.feedback_correct: That's the exact response in the playbook—clients don't interact with the software; they receive reports bearing your firm's name and brand.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course teaches that clients don't use your bookkeeping tool at all; they receive Excel reports signed by the firm. Familiarity with QuickBooks is irrelevant to the end product they see.

questions.question: What security reassurance should you give an owner who worries about an employee leaving with client data?
choices: Assure them that ESource monitors all employee activity continuously
Explain that only people the owner adds can sign in, employees lock out when removed, and books stay locked even on lost laptops
Promise that the system automatically alerts the owner whenever someone accesses client data
Recommend they require all staff to sign non-compete agreements
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—you've captured the security story: owner control, immediate lockout, and hardware-level protection mean clients always stay with the firm.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course teaches a specific security narrative: the owner controls access, removal is instantaneous and locks the computer, and backups are also locked to the firm. This directly addresses the fear of employee data theft.

questions.question: How should you close the deal, and what pilot size does the playbook recommend?
choices: Ask the firm to switch all clients immediately and sign a one-year contract
Propose a pilot of 3 to 5 clients for 60 days alongside their current system, with pre-agreed success measures
Offer a free trial for one client for 30 days with no commitment
Request that they sign up for the full system but allow them to migrate clients gradually over 6 months
questions.feedback_correct: That's the playbook: a small, safe pilot proves the value before any big commitment, and agreed-upon success measures make the transition clear.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes closing with a pilot, not a big switch. Three to five clients for 60 days, running alongside their current system, removes risk and builds confidence for a full rollout after success.

questions.question: What should you do before any pricing or contract is finalized with a prospect?
choices: Get approval from the prospect's CFO or bookkeeper
Confirm with Joe that the proposed pricing tiers are still current
Have the firm sign a non-disclosure agreement
Complete a full technical audit of their current systems
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the course emphasizes that pricing tiers are still proposed, so you must confirm with Joe before anything is signed to avoid misalignment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course explicitly instructs you to say 'proposed' when discussing pricing and to confirm with Joe before anything is signed. This protects both the firm and the integrity of your sales process.
